title: Six questions, looked back
hookLine: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe
carry: which one is quietly carrying you

cards: Six words could sum up this whole year: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Say them slowly and they sound like the chapter titles of a life. A person hurts.
Someone they love dies. They love, and get loved, imperfectly. They spend their days working at something.
They get wronged, and they wrong people. And now and then, the sky opens. This year asked each of those as a question, and handed it to the traditions willing to answer.
Today, the six side by side.

teach.b: First, the questions themselves. Why do people suffer? What happens when someone dies?
What is love? Why work? How do you forgive?
And what do you do with wonder? None of these were asked to be solved.

Each block brought voices from many traditions, scripture, philosophers, poets, scientists, and let them speak in their own words, each with its own name on it. Second, an old book that holds several at once.
Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible, says in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven".

teach.h: A TIME TO WEEP, A TIME TO DANCE.
teach.b: And a few lines later: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance". The writer doesn't rank the seasons.
Weeping and dancing both get their time, and this year gave suffering and awe, death and love, each a season of its own. Third, a poet's advice about questions.
Rainer Maria Rilke, writing letters to a young poet who wanted answers, told him to be patient with everything unsolved in his heart, and to try to love the questions themselves.

teach.h: WHICH ONE ARE YOU STILL CARRYING?
teach.b: Don't hunt for answers that can't be given yet, he said.
Live the questions, and maybe, gradually, you'll live your way into an answer. Fourth, why look back now. A year of big questions can blur.
Looking back doesn't mean deciding who was right. It means noticing which question you're still carrying, which one you put down, and which one is quietly carrying you.

how: People on a spiritual path of their own sometimes keep a journal and reread it at the end of a year; some synagogues read Ecclesiastes during the festival of Sukkot.

games.why: Rilke told him to love the questions themselves and live them, and perhaps live his way into an answer someday.

practice: Settle, and say the first word inside: suffering. Wait for whatever comes, a note you kept or a moment from that block, then go on, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe, without judging what shows up or what doesn't.
If you pray, offer each one up as it comes; if you don't, let each have its season.

wordCard.voice: Six questions. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: the year's questions, each given its own season, none of them solved. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: which one is quietly carrying you. None of the six needs an answer today. More tomorrow.
